evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §6: "`tp next`, `tp next --peek`, `tp ready` and `tp claim` on a bound task file read the graph first"; §9.5: "No change to `tp resume`'s phases". internal/engine/nextunits.go:40-66: "deriving emptiness from the blockers keeps the oracle from ever handing the driver a unit that cannot make progress" and the implement case calls `ImplementPreview(tf)`, which reads the task file only. REFERENCE.md:103: `next_units` is `[]` "when the phase is blocked".
finding: §6 gates only `tp next`, `tp next --peek`, `tp ready` and `tp claim` on the graph, and §9.5 keeps `tp resume`'s phases unchanged, but says nothing of `tp resume`'s `next_units`/`next_action`, `tp brief` or `tp run`. Implemented as written, a bound file whose epic has a dependency not done stays in phase `implement` with an implement unit in `next_units` (the oracle's subject comes from the task file alone), so `tp run` spawns a unit whose `tp next --brief` returns no task, the unit fails, and the driver retries a unit that cannot make progress. That breaks the oracle's existing invariant that it never hands the driver a unit that cannot progress.
suggestion: Add to §6 that `tp resume` (and so `tp brief`/`tp run`) reports the epic block as a blocker on a bound file: phase stays `implement`, `next_units` is `[]`, and the summary names `blocked_by_epics`, the same way it handles no ready task. Add a §10 row for it.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §3: "`done` | every bound file is at `release`" and "`done_at` is the done record's time, else the latest `closed_at` across the bound files"; §7: "`throughput`, epics reaching `done` per ISO week of `done_at`".
finding: An epic with bound files is `done` only once every bound file is at `release`, i.e. after its audit converges, but `done_at` is the latest task `closed_at`, which precedes the audit. So `done_at` names a time when the epic was not done, and `throughput` (per ISO week of `done_at`) books an epic in the week its tasks closed, not the week it became done: a past week's throughput changes when a later audit converges. This undoes for the timestamp what §10 row 2 guards for the status ("a status that reads `done` from the tasks alone, before the audit").
suggestion: Take `done_at` as the latest of the bound files' last `closed_at` and their last recorded audit round's `recorded_at`, or state that `done_at` is the work's close time and `throughput` counts work closed, not epics done.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:50 '`done` | every bound file is at `release`'; :52 '`release` is the phase `tp resume` already reports'; :72 'A gate is met once.'; internal/engine/phase.go:12-27 DetectPhase returns release only when auditConverged, and the comment states 'staleness (a stale spec reads unconverged)'; internal/engine/resume.go:90 AuditLoopDone(..., specHash).
finding: `done` for a bound epic is 'every bound file is at release', and release is tp resume's phase, which falls back to `audit` whenever the bound spec is edited after its audit converged (audit convergence reads false on a stale spec). A typo fix in a shipped epic's spec therefore turns the epic back to `in_progress`, turns its milestone's gate red although it carries a met record, and closes every later milestone of the track again. That contradicts §4 'A gate is met once' and §9.2 'a gate or a condition is met once': the spec never says whether a green gate may go red through a member's derived status, and two implementations (re-derive always vs. latch done at first release) would disagree on every later milestone's openness.
suggestion: Decide it in §3/§4: either state that an epic's status (and so a gate) may regress when a bound spec goes stale and that later milestones close again, or latch `done` (e.g. done_at once reached at release) so a post-release spec edit does not reopen it; add a §10 row for the chosen behaviour.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:70-71, :94-95; skills/tp/SKILL.md:713 'epics in no track's milestone follow in their own tables'.
finding: Openness is defined only for epics in a track's milestone ('A milestone is open when every earlier milestone of its track has a green gate'), and `tp epic ready` requires 'in an open milestone'. The graph allows epics in no track's milestone (the existing `tp epic export --md` prints them in their own tables), so whether such an epic is ever ready without `--all` is unstated: one implementation treats it as always open, another never lists it.
suggestion: State whether an epic in no milestone is open (ready on its dependencies alone) or excluded from `tp epic ready` without `--all`.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:17-18 '3. Gates open milestones. ... only an open milestone's epics are ready'; :23-24 '5. ... consult the epic's dependencies: while one is not done, no task of the file is ready'; :87-89 §6 names only dependencies. §10 row 3 tests only the dependency case.
finding: Whether a bound task file's tasks are held back by a closed milestone is read two ways. §1 item 3 says 'only an open milestone's epics are ready' and §1 frames the release as connecting 'milestone order, gates and dependencies' to the work, but §1 item 5 and §6 make `tp next`/`tp ready`/`tp claim` consult only the epic's dependencies. One implementation returns the task of a file bound to an epic in a closed milestone (whose dependencies are done); another, reading §1.3, reports it blocked. Their tests on that fixture disagree, and `blocked_by_epics` has no way to name a gate as the blocker.
suggestion: State in §6 whether the open-milestone rule applies to a bound file's tasks; if it does not, say so explicitly (a bound file in a closed milestone is ready once its epic's dependencies are done).

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:17-18 'A milestone is open when every earlier milestone of its track has a green gate; only an open milestone's epics are ready.'; :87-89 '`tp next` ... read the graph first: while any dependency of the file's epic is not `done`, no task is ready'; :33-35 binding refusals list no milestone condition; spec/1.3.0.md:96 later-milestone-dependency fires only on edges into a later milestone.
finding: §1 item 3 says 'only an open milestone's epics are ready', and §1 item 5 / §6 say the task layer gates a bound file only on its epic's dependencies. Nothing refuses binding a file to an epic of a closed milestone (§2 refuses only absent, condition and done epics), and later-milestone-dependency lint means a B epic's edges point back into A or nowhere, so a file bound to a dependency-free epic of milestone B gets ready tasks from `tp next`/`tp claim` while A's gate is red. One implementer reads §6 as exhaustive (tasks start); another applies §1.3's open-milestone rule to `tp next` as well (blocked). The release's stated goal is that 'what can start now' is no longer read by hand from milestone order, gates and dependencies, which the first reading leaves half true.
suggestion: State in §6 whether a bound file of an epic in a closed milestone is blocked (and under what key in the response, e.g. alongside blocked_by_epics), or state explicitly that milestone order gates only `tp epic ready` and not the task layer.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §1.3: "A milestone is open when every earlier milestone of its track has a green gate; only an open milestone's epics are ready." §6: "while any dependency of the file's epic is not `done`, no task is ready". §2 binding refusals: "when the graph does not hold the id, when the epic is a condition, or when the epic carries a done record".
finding: §1.3 says "only an open milestone's epics are ready", and §6 is titled "The graph gates the work", but §6 blocks a bound file's tasks only on the epic's dependencies. A task file bound to an epic of a milestone that is not open (earlier gate red, threshold unmet) has ready tasks, and §2 does not refuse such a binding. So the milestone gate gates `tp epic ready` but not the work, and an agent working from `tp next` starts work the gate was meant to hold back.
suggestion: Either add the closed-milestone case to §6's block (with the closed milestone named in the response), or state in §1/§6 that milestone order gates only `tp epic ready` and that a binding is the operator's choice to start early.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:33-35 (refusals only on `tp init --epic`/`tp set --epic`); :87-90 (§6 covers bound and unbound files only).
finding: §2 refuses a binding to an absent id, a condition, or a done-recorded epic, but only at binding time. The graph is edited afterwards (epics renamed, removed, or set `condition: true`), and §6 does not say what `tp next`/`tp ready`/`tp claim` and §3 status do when a bound file's `epic` names an id the graph no longer holds, or when no graph file exists. One implementation treats the file as unbound (v1.4.2 behaviour), another refuses or reports it blocked; their tests disagree.
suggestion: State the behaviour of a dangling binding (e.g. refused with a hint, or reported as blocked) for the task commands and for `tp epic status`/`export`.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:94-97; §3 table :46 defines `planned` as 'no bound file, no done record, no claim', which the ready rule does not reference.
finding: The `tp epic ready` criteria for work epics ('in an open milestone, every dependency done, no bound file, no claim, not a condition') never exclude an epic that already carries a done record: a taskless epic marked done with `tp epic done` meets every listed criterion and a literal implementation lists it as ready. Likewise 'the conditions whose own dependencies are done are listed apart, as waiting on the operator' does not exclude a condition already done, and does not say whether the open-milestone rule (and `--all`) applies to conditions, so a condition opening milestone B is listed before A's gate is green by one implementation and not by another.
suggestion: Define the ready work epics as `planned` epics meeting the milestone and dependency rules, the waiting conditions as not-done conditions whose dependencies are done, and state whether the milestone rule applies to conditions.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:104-105; §10 row 12 checks only the by-count path on a single-milestone chain, so it cannot tell the readings apart.
finding: `critical_path` is defined as 'the longest chain of not-done epics to the milestone's gate, by count, and by summed estimate when every epic on it has one'. Two readings: (a) one chain, the longest by count, whose estimates are then summed; (b) two separately computed paths, the longest by count and the heaviest by summed estimate, which can be different chains. It is also unstated whether the chain may run through not-done epics of earlier milestones or other tracks that a gate member depends on, or stays inside the milestone. Implementations choosing differently report different paths on the same graph.
suggestion: Say whether the estimate figure is the sum over the by-count chain or the heaviest chain by estimate, and whether chains are bounded to the milestone's own epics.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §7: "`tp epic claim <id> [--by <name>]` writes `claimed: {at, by}` under the file's lock and exits 1 when a claim exists"; §5: "it cannot be claimed" (conditions only); §6: "`tp claim` exits 1" while a dependency is not done.
finding: `tp epic claim` is refused only when a claim exists (and, by §5, on a condition). The spec does not say whether it refuses an epic with a bound file, a done epic, an epic with a dependency not done, or one in a milestone that is not open. §6 refuses `tp claim` on a task whose epic is blocked, so claiming the blocked epic itself is either the same rule one level up or deliberately allowed. Two implementations disagree, and §10 row 11 covers only the double claim.
suggestion: State the claim preconditions: either 'only an epic `tp epic ready --all` lists', or the explicit list (not done, no bound file, dependencies done?), and add the chosen refusals to row 11.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:111-114 'it lists every epic review slice with its key ... each epic review state directory records its slice's key for it'; internal/engine/epicstatedir.go:17-18 EpicReviewStateDir = filepath.Join(tpDir, "epic-review", epicHash(epicSliceKeyText(key))) — the directory name is a hash of the key.
finding: `tp epic export` 'lists every epic review slice with its key', and the key is supplied by 'each epic review state directory records its slice's key for it' — a new write. Slice directories recorded under v1.3/v1.4 are named by a one-way hash of the key and hold no key, so for them the requirement cannot be satisfied as written. The spec does not say whether export omits such slices, lists them keyless, or backfills the key on the next emission/record, and §8 'A file without them reads as before' covers task and graph files only.
suggestion: Add one sentence for pre-1.5 slice directories: e.g. export lists them with `key: null` (or skips them) until the next round of that slice writes the key; and a §10 row or a clause in row 13 for a keyless directory.

evidence: internal/engine/epicstatedir.go:17-18: `filepath.Join(tpDir, EpicReviewStateRoot, epicHash(epicSliceKeyText(key)))`, a one-way hash. spec/1.5.0.md §7: "it lists every epic review slice with its key and state ... each epic review state directory records its slice's key for it."
finding: `tp epic export` must list "every epic review slice with its key", and the spec says each state directory records its key. Epic review state directories are named by a SHA-256 of the key, so a directory recorded before v1.5.0 carries no key and its key cannot be recovered from its name. Export either drops those slices or lists them without a key; the spec says neither, and §8's "A file without them reads as before" covers the task and graph files only.
suggestion: Say what happens to a pre-1.5.0 directory: the key is written on its next emission or record (and export lists it flagged without a key until then), or export recovers it by matching hashes of the graph's current milestones and epics.

evidence: internal/engine/epicstatedir.go:18 `filepath.Join(tpDir, EpicReviewStateRoot, epicHash(epicSliceKeyText(key)))` — the directory name is a hash; spec/1.5.0.md:111-114; spec/1.5.0-measurements.md:54 (pilot review rounds).
finding: `tp epic export` must list 'every epic review slice with its key and state', and the release adds that 'each epic review state directory records its slice's key'. Slice directories recorded by v1.3/v1.4 are named by a one-way hash of the key and hold no key, so for them the requirement cannot be met without a migration the spec does not mention; one implementation omits such slices, another lists them keyless, another fails. The requesting project already ran epic review rounds in the v1.4 pilot, so such directories exist in the field.
suggestion: Say how a pre-1.5.0 slice directory without a recorded key appears in the export (listed with a null key, or keyed on its next round), or require a migration.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §7: "lists the work epics that can start: in an open milestone, every dependency `done`, no bound file, no claim, not a condition. The conditions whose own dependencies are done are listed apart"; §5: "`tp epic done <id> --evidence` writes `done: {at, evidence}` on an epic with no bound file, condition or not".
finding: `tp epic ready`'s criteria are "in an open milestone, every dependency `done`, no bound file, no claim, not a condition". A work epic marked done by `tp epic done` (which §5 allows on any epic with no bound file) meets all of them, so read literally it stays in the ready list after it is done. The same holds for the conditions "whose own dependencies are done", which are listed as waiting on the operator after their done record exists. Two correct implementations disagree on whether done epics appear.
suggestion: Define the ready list by status: work epics whose status is `planned`, in an open milestone, with every dependency `done`; and conditions whose status is not `done` and whose dependencies are done.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §7 line 102-107: "`tp epic status [--milestone <m>]` reports, per milestone: ... `critical_path` ... `throughput`, epics reaching `done` per ISO week of `done_at`; and the estimate-versus-actual roll-up"; §7 line 110-113: "The JSON carries a schema `version` and every derived field ... It is the contract a view of the plan reads"; spec/1.5.0-measurements.md lists these as "Its priorities for the view", i.e. for the dashboard reader, not the agent.
finding: `tp epic status` carries view-only metrics — `critical_path` by summed estimate, `throughput` per ISO week of `done_at`, and the estimate-versus-actual roll-up — that no agent decision reads (an agent chooses what to start from the ready/blocked lists and the gate state, and stops on what waits on the operator). The same derived fields are also required in `tp epic export`, which §7 names as the contract a view of the plan reads, so every agent call to `tp epic status` pays for dashboard bytes the export already serves.
suggestion: Keep throughput, the estimate-versus-actual roll-up and the estimate-weighted critical path in `tp epic export` only; `tp epic status` reports per milestone whether it is open, counts and share done, the gate's state, the ready and blocked lists and what waits on the operator (or strips the view metrics under `--compact`).

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §8: "`claimed`, `done` and `met` are written only by their commands." skills/tp/SKILL.md:715 (`add --bulk`): "a row whose `id` exists replaces that epic in place"; :717: "`tp epic set <milestones|gates|tag_checks>=<json>` Replace that whole top-level object"; :720 `tp epic import`: "Replace `.tp/epics.json` with `<file>`, a graph in the file's own shape".
finding: §8 says `claimed`, `done` and `met` are written only by their commands, but existing graph writers replace whole objects: `tp epic set gates=<json>` replaces every gate (dropping or forging `met`), `tp epic import` writes a whole graph in the file's shape, and `tp epic add --bulk` replaces an existing epic in place (dropping `claimed`/`done`). The spec does not say whether these writers refuse, preserve or carry these fields, so the rule cannot hold as written, and an ordinary gate edit erases a recorded met.
suggestion: State the rule for the existing writers: they carry `claimed`, `done` and `met` over from the file as it stands and refuse a payload that sets them (or name the one exception, e.g. `import --force` restoring a backup).

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md:141 row 2 fixture 'the chain, one file bound to b'; :89 'and `tp claim` exits 1'; spec/1.3.0.md:186 '`x → y` means `x` depends on `y`' and the chain is a → b → c → d, so b depends on c.
finding: Row 2 drives b's file to `in_progress` 'once a task is `wip`' on the fixture 'the chain, one file bound to b', where c (b's dependency) is not done. By §6, `tp claim` on that file exits 1 while c is not done, so the row cannot reach `wip` through tp's own commands with that fixture.
suggestion: Make row 2's fixture record c done (`tp epic done c`) before the claim step, or state that the wip status is written by hand in the fixture.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §2 line 40: "A binding clears the epic's claim."; §3 rows: `claimed` holds only with "no bound file", `specced` holds with "a bound file" regardless of claim; §7 line 94-95: ready requires "no bound file, no claim".
finding: "A binding clears the epic's claim" makes `tp set --epic` write a second file (the graph) for state the status derivation already ignores: once a file is bound the epic is `specced`/`in_progress`/`done` whatever its claim (§3), and `tp epic ready` already excludes epics with a bound file (§7). The write feeds no decision and adds a cross-file mutation and lock to a task-file writer; it also leaves `tp set --epic ""` reading two ways (does the unbound epic return to `planned` or keep nothing to return to).
suggestion: Delete the clearing write; let the derivation ignore `claimed` while a bound file exists (it already does per §3), so `tp set --epic` touches only the task file.

evidence: spec/1.5.0.md §7: "Under `TP_UNATTENDED`, `tp epic done`, `tp epic gate --met` and `tp set --epic` exit 2". CLAUDE.md rule 9: "the unit records it with `tp escalate --decision <name>` (the closed set is `engine.EscalationDecisions`)". internal/cli/epic_review_record.go:39 refuses with `engine.EscalateOther`.
finding: §7 adds three operator decisions that exit 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED` (`tp epic done`, `tp epic gate --met`, `tp set --epic`), but does not say how a unit records them. The project's rule is that a unit hitting such an exit records it with `tp escalate --decision <name>` from the closed set `engine.EscalationDecisions`; without a name for these, the unit either cannot escalate or files them under a generic decision.
suggestion: State which escalation decision each refusal names (new members of the set, or the existing generic one), so the refusal hint and `tp escalate` agree.

evidence: internal/engine/epicslice.go:197-226: `epicBlock` renders id, title, milestone, tags, acceptance, depends_on; `epicGateBlock` renders members and deferrable. spec/1.5.0.md §8: "An epic gains `condition` ... a gate gains `threshold` and `met`"; §4: "A gate may carry `threshold`, the exit condition in the operator's words."
finding: `condition` changes what an epic means (no spec, done by the operator) and a gate's `threshold` is the operator's exit condition, yet the spec does not say whether either enters the epic review unit. Today the unit block whitelists id, title, milestone, tags, acceptance and edges, and the gate block members and deferrable, so a graph review would grade a condition as a work epic and never see a threshold, and editing either would not stale a converged slice.
suggestion: Say in §8 that `condition` and `threshold` are part of the reviewed unit (and `claimed`, `done`, `met`, `estimate_minutes` are not), so a review sees them and an edit stales the slice.
